patterns.situation: A user reports a charge they do not recognize, often in a public, alarmed tone.
patterns.reply_strategy: Acknowledge in one clause, then hand them the self-serve path to dispute that specific transaction inside the app, and offer a human review as the second step.
do: Point to the exact in-app action (open the transaction, report it)
Offer a second step for anything the self-serve path does not settle
Keep account specifics out of the thread
dont: Ask for card numbers, dates or amounts in the reply
State whether the charge is valid
Promise a refund or a chargeback outcome
patterns.example_case: User sees a payment to a merchant they never used and has already frozen their card. Developer says an unrecognized payment can be reported from the transaction screen and offers a review of related card fees via its support address.

patterns.situation: The purchase was billed by the app store, so the developer cannot issue the refund themselves.
patterns.reply_strategy: Say plainly who owns the billing relationship (the app store), name the store's refund process, and link the help article that explains it. Do not pretend you can refund it.
do: State the boundary in the first sentence
Name the store's refund or dispute flow
Link one help article on store-managed subscriptions
dont: Apologize as if you will refund it
Send them to a generic support home page
Debate whether the trial terms were clear
patterns.example_case: User was billed a yearly fee after a trial and says both the developer and the store refused a refund. Developer explains the subscription is managed by the store where it was bought and points to that store's refund process plus an article on app-store subscriptions.

patterns.situation: User objects to how much of the product sits behind a paywall, not to a specific charge.
patterns.reply_strategy: Explain the boundary factually (what is free, how to recognize a paid item before using it, how to swap it for a free one). No persuasion, no discount pitch.
do: Name the visual marker that identifies paid items
Give the one-step way to avoid the charge
Stay neutral about pricing
dont: Argue the price is fair
Upsell the paid plan
Repeat the same paragraph to every pricing complaint
patterns.example_case: User says a design tool now charges for basic actions. Developer explains that installing costs nothing, paid items carry a crown icon before you add them, and any paid item can be swapped for a free alternative.

patterns.situation: User alleges hidden or unfair fees but gives no specifics you could check.
patterns.reply_strategy: Say you want to look at the specific charges, and ask them to write from their registered email with the fees in question. Move the dispute off the public thread.
do: Ask for the specific fees, not the whole story
Require the registered/contact email so the right account is reviewed
Acknowledge the trust damage without admitting fault
dont: Defend the fee schedule publicly
Deny that the fees exist
Publish fee breakdowns that reveal the user's account
patterns.example_case: User accuses a neobank of hidden charges and says they have lost all trust. Developer says it would like to review the charges mentioned and asks for an email from the address linked to the account.

patterns.situation: Funds are stuck in transit and the user names a real-world consequence.
patterns.reply_strategy: Name the urgency back to them, give one neutral sentence on what can affect transfer timing, and route to a specialist who can see that specific transfer.
do: Acknowledge the consequence, not just the delay
Offer a brief, non-blaming explanation of what affects timing
Route to a team that can inspect the individual transfer
dont: Give an estimated arrival time
Blame the sending bank or the user
Reply with the generic 'contact support' line
patterns.example_case: A transfer meant to cover a hospital bill took days to land and carried large fees. Developer acknowledges the frustration in an urgent situation, notes that timing and intermediary fees depend on the transfer rail, and asks for registered details so a specialist can look into that transfer.

patterns.situation: A paid-for 'instant' option did not behave as advertised and the user is stranded mid-transaction.
patterns.reply_strategy: Recognize that earlier support may not have resolved it, then offer a fresh look through a dedicated link. Frame it as a second attempt, not a first contact.
do: Acknowledge that prior help may have fallen short
Use a dedicated, issue-specific support link
Keep the first sentence about the user's situation, not your brand
dont: Explain how instant transfers normally work
Ask them to redo troubleshooting they already did
Use the same link you post under every review
patterns.example_case: Stranded at a gas station, a user chose the instant deposit option and the money stayed pending. Developer says it may not have given the help expected before and offers a second chance through a separate support link.

patterns.situation: A refund was refused or a cancellation term is disputed. The developer's verdict and the user's story conflict.
patterns.reply_strategy: Acknowledge the disagreement, say you would like to look into it, and ask for the booking reference through a channel where records can be checked. Never rule on the case in the reply.
do: Ask for the itinerary or order reference
Use a neutral verb ('look into', 'review')
Keep it short; long replies read as stonewalling
dont: Restate the cancellation policy as the answer
Say the refund was correctly denied
Repeat the same paragraph across dozens of reviews
patterns.example_case: User says a booking shown as refundable was partly non-refundable and a refund has not arrived. Developer says it wants to review the matter but cannot message reviewers directly on the store, and gives one support URL.

patterns.situation: The price the user saw is not the price they paid. This is both a product complaint and a charge dispute.
patterns.reply_strategy: Handle both halves: tell them the pricing feedback is being passed to the product team, and separately route the specific booking to support. One sentence each.
do: Separate the product issue from the individual charge
Give a channel for the individual charge
Avoid defending the price display
dont: Explain how taxes and fees are displayed
Only collect the feedback and ignore the charge
Only route to support and ignore the display bug
patterns.example_case: User complains that the headline price hides taxes and fees until the card screen. Developer thanks them for the pricing feedback, says it cannot promise immediate changes, and offers a support route for the specific booking.

patterns.situation: The disputed charge belongs to one order. A general support entry point forces the user to re-find the order.
patterns.reply_strategy: Give the tap-by-tap path from the order record to a support conversation, so the agent arrives with the order already in context.
do: Start the path from the order, not from the help menu
Write it as an explicit breadcrumb (Screen > Item > Action)
State what the team will do once there (review the transaction)
dont: Say 'contact customer service' with no path
Mix order issues and app bugs in one route
Send the same breadcrumb to a complaint it does not fit
patterns.example_case: User was billed twice for one item at self-checkout and the app's return flow has no matching reason. Developer gives a path from purchase history to the specific order and its support chat so the transaction can be reviewed.

patterns.situation: A product feature automatically withdrew money and the user says it cost them something essential.
patterns.reply_strategy: Acknowledge the severity of the concrete consequence in plain words before anything else. Then invite them to a review of that feature's transactions.
do: Acknowledge severity explicitly
Name the feature so they know you read the review
Offer a review of the transactions in question
dont: Explain how the feature is designed to work
Lead with policy language
Scale the stakes down ('we understand your frustration')
patterns.example_case: A repayment feature took two incoming payments minutes apart and the user says it cost them money for food. Developer says it understands the severity of the situation, names the feature, and offers a review of those transactions.

patterns.situation: A credit the user is owed cannot be redeemed in the checkout flow.
patterns.reply_strategy: Treat it as a technical account issue: say it is being investigated and ask for the booking details through the support channel.
do: Say the specific failure is being investigated
Ask for booking or itinerary details
Offer one channel
dont: Explain credit terms
Tell them to try again later
Ignore the redemption failure and only apologize
patterns.example_case: User holds flight credit that the app will not apply at checkout, and chat and phone support are both unreachable. Developer says the issue is being investigated and points to a chat route to a live agent.

patterns.situation: The account was closed for a policy violation and the user says they were never told what they did.
patterns.reply_strategy: Recognize that a closure is hard news, link the terms so the user can read the policy themselves, and give the appeal route. Do not state the violation publicly.
do: Link the terms of service
Offer a route to request more information or appeal
Keep the tone neutral, not defensive
dont: Name the suspected violation in public
Say the decision is final with no next step
Copy a generic 'reach out here' line
patterns.example_case: User says the account was deactivated with only a vague policy reference. Developer notes there are many possible reasons for a closure, links its terms of service, and offers a separate contact option for further help.

patterns.situation: A regulated financial account was closed and the user demands a reason in public.
patterns.reply_strategy: State three things in order: decisions follow review and regulatory requirements, specifics cannot be discussed in public, and a registered-email channel exists for clarification.
do: Explain the regulatory frame in one sentence
State the public/private boundary explicitly
Give the exact channel (registered email address)
dont: Hint at the reason
Argue with the accusation
Leave 'final' as the last word with no channel
patterns.example_case: A long-standing personal and business customer says both accounts were closed with no meaningful explanation. Developer says closure decisions follow careful review and regulatory requirements, that specifics cannot be discussed on public platforms, and gives a support address for further clarification.

patterns.situation: The account keeps getting restricted pending the same identity or funding checks.
patterns.reply_strategy: Explain in one sentence why the check is required (security, regulation), then ask them to write in so the specific pattern can be reviewed.
do: Give the reason for the check
Acknowledge the repetition is frustrating
Offer a review of why it keeps recurring
dont: Repeat 'we must comply with regulations' alone
Tell them to submit the documents again
Imply the user did something wrong
patterns.example_case: User says the account was frozen repeatedly while adding money with another bank's card and the same documents were requested each time. Developer explains top-up cards must be verified as a regulated institution and asks for an email to look closer.

patterns.situation: A security check rejects the user's device and they insist the device is ordinary.
patterns.reply_strategy: State the check that is failing and why it exists, give two or three concrete things to try, and offer a channel if it persists.
do: Name the check (official software, device integrity)
Give ordered steps (clear data, restart, retry)
Offer a next step if it still fails
dont: Accuse the user of modifying the device
Only say the device is unsupported
Suggest bypassing the check
patterns.example_case: User cannot update a banking app because it reports a rooted device. Developer explains the app requires official manufacturer software for security reasons and lists steps to try before contacting support.

patterns.situation: An age gate is blocking an adult user who has already paid or verified elsewhere.
patterns.reply_strategy: Give the exact settings path to correct the age group, list the accepted verification methods, and mention that a failed method can be retried with another.
do: Give the settings path to fix it
List the verification methods accepted
Mention the retry/alternative option
dont: Explain why age verification exists at length
Send them to a general contact page without the path
Doubt the user's stated age
patterns.example_case: Long-time paying user fails an age check despite a card on file and a stated birth date. Developer gives the settings location for confirming age, lists several accepted methods, and notes another method can be chosen if one fails.

patterns.situation: The account was restricted because of a group or server it belonged to, not for the user's own actions.
patterns.reply_strategy: Acknowledge why that feels unfair, then point to the formal review request in the violation notice.
do: Acknowledge the user's feeling of being blamed for others
Point to the review link in the notice itself
Offer a second route if the notice is missing
dont: Defend the enforcement action
Discuss the group's content
Tell them the restriction is permanent
patterns.example_case: User's account was restricted because of a server joined a year earlier that they no longer read. Developer acknowledges the frustration and explains how to ask for the violation to be reviewed, from the notice or the help site.

patterns.situation: User says the suspension came with no reason, but the reason is visible in the product.
patterns.reply_strategy: Tell them where in settings the account standing and reason are shown, then where to get help with the remaining steps.
do: Name the settings screen that shows the status
Give the help route for the part that needs a human
Keep it short
dont: Say 'we take safety seriously'
Ask them to describe the violation
Send them to a forum
patterns.example_case: User says an account was suspended without warning right after sign-up. Developer says to check the account standing section in settings for details and gives a help link for registration or verification problems.

patterns.situation: The sign-in or verification code never reaches the user.
patterns.reply_strategy: Give the two or three most likely causes as checks (wrong address, spam folder), then a fallback link with more steps, then a support contact.
do: Address the user by name if the store shows it
Order checks from most to least likely
End with a support contact, not just an article
dont: Only say 'check your spam folder'
Offer to send the code yourself
Suggest creating a new account
patterns.example_case: User cannot get a login code for a school account and needs it urgently. Developer tells them to check spam and confirm the address, links troubleshooting steps, and offers a support contact to take a closer look.

patterns.situation: The user cannot sign in, most likely because they are using a different method or address than at sign-up.
patterns.reply_strategy: State the likely cause as a check (same email and sign-in method as when the account was created), then link a dedicated recovery page.
do: Frame the cause as something to check, not a diagnosis
Link a page dedicated to sign-in problems
Keep it to two sentences
dont: Reset the password for them or ask for it
List every possible cause
Route to a general help center
patterns.example_case: User cannot sign in with a phone number because the code arrived through a different channel. Developer suggests using the same email and sign-in method used to create the account and links a recovery page.

patterns.situation: A verification link or QR flow loops and never completes. There is a specific, non-obvious technical cause.
patterns.reply_strategy: Name the exact condition that breaks the flow and the workaround, then ask for a screen recording if it still fails.
do: Name the specific cause (same device, same profile, newest link only)
Give a workaround
Ask for a screen recording rather than a description
dont: Say 'try again later'
Resend the same instructions
Blame the user's connection
patterns.example_case: User taps a verify-email button and the app keeps demanding verification. Developer explains the link only works on the same phone and profile as the app and only the newest link is valid, gives a copy-paste workaround, and asks for a recording if still stuck.

patterns.situation: The user wants an old account back and no longer controls the original email or phone. Recovery cannot be done from a review reply.
patterns.reply_strategy: Say upfront that it has to be handled inside the app, then give a numbered tap path to report the problem. Do not discuss the account.
do: State that the store reply cannot resolve it
Give a numbered in-app path
Acknowledge the wait
dont: Ask for the old email, phone or password
Promise the account will be restored
Reply with a feature-request template
patterns.example_case: User knows an old account's credentials but recovery demands a phone number from years ago. Developer gives numbered steps to report the problem from the profile menu.

patterns.situation: A creator believes the algorithm is suppressing them and describes it as a penalty.
patterns.reply_strategy: Treat it as a reportable account problem: apologize for the inconvenience and route to the in-app report path. Do not debate how the algorithm works.
do: Use the same in-app report route as for lockouts
Avoid confirming or denying a 'ban'
Keep it short
dont: Explain the recommendation algorithm
Say there is no such thing as a shadowban
Reply with the feature-request template
patterns.example_case: Creator reports no engagement and suspects the device is flagged. Developer apologizes for the inconvenience and gives the in-app path to report the issue.

patterns.situation: The review is about the developer's previous reply or support, not the product. A standard reply here confirms the user's point.
patterns.reply_strategy: Say directly that earlier help may not have resolved it, use the user's name if available, and offer to look again. Drop the boilerplate.
do: Acknowledge the earlier support failure in plain words
Address the user by name where the store shows it
Offer a fresh look rather than restating the standard line
dont: Reuse the standard 'we are here to help' sentence
Defend the support team
Pretend this is first contact
patterns.example_case: User says support closed the chat without solving the problem and asks the developer not to reply that it is here to help. Developer says the user may not have received the help hoped for before and offers to look into it further.

patterns.situation: The user is trapped in an automated support loop and says so.
patterns.reply_strategy: Acknowledge the automated agent specifically, say it is being looked at, and describe how to reach a human agent from the support page.
do: Name the automation the user complained about
Describe the click that reaches a human
Keep the apology specific
dont: Send them back into the same chat without saying how to get a human
Deny or ignore the automation
Use the general 'contact support' line
patterns.example_case: User says a virtual agent repeats wrong answers and a confirmed refund has not arrived. Developer acknowledges the feedback about the virtual agent and explains which option on the support page connects to a live agent.

patterns.situation: The case needs details the user will not post publicly, and the store does not let developers message reviewers.
patterns.reply_strategy: Say in the first or second sentence that you cannot message directly on the store, then give one channel and list exactly which details to bring.
do: State the no-direct-message limit explicitly
Give exactly one channel
List what to include (reference number, itinerary, device model)
dont: Say 'we are always here to help' without a channel
Give three or four channels at once
Ask for details in the public reply
patterns.example_case: User's booking changed dates after the app froze at checkout. Developer says direct messaging is not available on the store and asks for name and itinerary details through the support site.

patterns.situation: A blocking technical problem with too little information to act on.
patterns.reply_strategy: Acknowledge what is blocked, then ask for the three things that make a bug reproducible: device model, app or OS version, and what happens on screen.
do: Ask for device, version and observed behaviour
Say what blocked them in their words
Give one contact route
dont: Give a troubleshooting ladder before asking anything
Use a generic 'sorry for the inconvenience' with no question
Ask for logs in the public reply
patterns.example_case: User cannot reach their money because the app freezes at sign-in after an update. Developer asks them to email their device model, app version and what they see on screen.

patterns.situation: A common technical symptom that the standard steps resolve most of the time.
patterns.reply_strategy: List three or four ordered steps (update, restart, clear cache, reinstall), then one escalation route for when they fail.
do: Order steps from least to most disruptive
Include the platform-specific path (settings > apps > storage)
End with an escalation route
dont: List more than four steps
Omit the escalation and stop at 'reinstall'
Give steps that do not match the symptom
patterns.example_case: User reports a group-payment button that stopped working. Developer suggests updating, clearing the app cache via the device settings path and restarting, then the in-app chat if it persists.

patterns.situation: The symptom matches a known issue with a dedicated help article.
patterns.reply_strategy: Restate the symptom as the user experienced it, then name the article by its symptom so they can find it even if the link breaks.
do: Restate the symptom in the user's terms
Name the help topic by symptom
Give one concrete next action
dont: Link an unrelated or generic article
Name the article by internal jargon
Send a bare link with no sentence
patterns.example_case: User says a downloaded design differs from the editor. Developer restates that, points to the help topic on designs looking different after download, and suggests trying another supported format.

patterns.situation: A paying subscriber hits a problem that free users would tolerate.
patterns.reply_strategy: Say you would like to investigate, and ask them to contact support with a screenshot of the review and reply so the agent has context.
do: Recognize they are paying
Ask them to bring the review thread to support
Offer social or messaging channels where they exist
dont: Treat it like a free-tier complaint
Only give troubleshooting steps
Explain ad policy at length
patterns.example_case: Paying listener still hears ads in podcasts and was told it is a feature. Developer asks them to contact support again with a screenshot of the review and reply, and lists the social handles and live messaging route.

patterns.situation: The user has already been through support more than once.
patterns.reply_strategy: Offer a distinct entry point from the one that failed and frame it as a second attempt at supporting them.
do: Use a different link from the general support page
Frame it as another chance to help
Keep it to two sentences
dont: Send them back to the same queue without acknowledging it
Ask them to open a new ticket and re-explain
Promise a specific resolution
patterns.example_case: User updates a review to say repeated calls produced no help. Developer offers the chance to change their mind by providing the support they deserve through a separate link.

patterns.situation: The complaint is about data quality that needs structured, in-product reporting rather than a conversation.
patterns.reply_strategy: Ask the user to submit the details through the in-app report so the right team gets structured data, and optionally point to a help community.
do: Say why the in-app report is better than a reply (structured details)
Address the user by name
Offer the forum as a second option, not the only one
dont: Send everyone to a forum where threads get locked
Give a generic 'we value your feedback' with no action
Use the same forum link for unrelated complaints
patterns.example_case: User reports misleading map data and misleading route times. Developer says it would like to learn more and asks for a post in the help community, after suggesting the in-app report that routes details to the product team.

patterns.situation: The review is a feature request or a complaint about a removed feature.
patterns.reply_strategy: Send it to a public feedback board where requests can be upvoted, so the user can see it was logged.
do: Give the feedback board URL
Say 'post or upvote' so they know it is a public log
Keep it short
dont: Use it for bug reports or account problems
Promise the feature will ship
Reply to an outage with a feedback link
patterns.example_case: User mourns a removed swipe gesture used daily. Developer points to the feedback site for posting or upvoting the change request.

patterns.situation: A UI change makes the product harder to use for someone with an accessibility need.
patterns.reply_strategy: Acknowledge the specific need, give the settings that help today, state honestly what is still limited, and ask for the feedback on the board.
do: Acknowledge the specific accessibility need
Give the available settings (font size, contrast)
Say plainly what is not yet available
dont: Say accessibility is a priority with no action
Ignore the workaround and only give the board
Argue the new design is better
patterns.example_case: User with dyslexia says a redesign's smaller font causes eye strain. Developer names the accessibility settings that help today, says font options are limited for now, and asks for the feedback on its board.
